rationale:
Evidence: iteration 2 (body 0.18 x 0.12 m, 0.8 kg, sensors at y 0.06, x -0.06 to +0.06, 16 mm footprints, kp 3.0, ki 0.3, kd 0.4, base_speed 1.6, last_direction) is still the best design (score 132.0). It has the highest progress on all three tracks (oval 0.45, s-bend 0.27, slalom 0.16) and the only finish (oval, 1.88 s). Iteration 4 resubmitted it and matched exactly, so the identical scores are a real repeat of the same design, not a logging fault. Max error sits at about 0.06 m on every track and seed, rms is flat at about 0.03 m, and progress stalls. Line loss is 0.05 on the oval but 0.65 on the s-bend and 0.8 on the slalom.

What I accepted from the round-1 critique: (1) The draft changed four geometry fields plus the sensor row at once, so its result could not be attributed to inertia, lead or mass. I reject that draft as the candidate. (2) The body_width argument was wrong: the off-track limit is 0.06 m for any width below 0.19 m, so width is not a lever. (3) The steady max_error with flat rms points to something other than gain-driven overshoot, and the iteration-4 decision rule said that if progress stays flat, the next single-variable test is base_speed 1.8. (4) Speed is not clearly binding on the oval (1.88 s finish), but a faster run also moves toward the 3.0 s completion and time terms, and the time term is worth up to 60 points.

What I rejected: (a) The mass, length and width reduction. Its inertia arithmetic is correct (about 60 percent lower yaw inertia), but mass also changes traction, slip and motor loading, which the draft did not model. Reverting this keeps the test clean. (b) The draft's sensor move to y 0.07. The extra 1 cm of lead is small and not isolated. (c) ki 0 and ki 0.6 were already tested, with ki 0.6 scoring lower (122.2), so I keep ki 0.3. (d) kp and kd changes: kp 2.8 and kd 1.0 were both shown to add no reliable gain.

What I changed: base_speed from 1.6 to 1.8, with geometry and every other controller field identical to iteration 2. This is a single-variable test. Expected result: completion_time on the oval well under 1.88 s, more progress on the s-bend and slalom if the robot can hold the line at the higher speed, and possibly more off-track ends if lateral load is the limit. Decision rule for the next round: if progress rises and the run stays on track, the next step is to keep 1.8 and test whether the line-loss events on the s-bend and slalom fall. If progress falls or off-track ends rise sooner, return to 1.6 and test a sensor footprint or span change on the s-bend and slalom. If max_error still reaches 0.06 with flat rms at 1.8, the cause is the steady bias, so the next test is a smaller ki (about 0.1) on its own.
